english.html: of a city, of a country or of a province <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>, and nevertheless, to make it appear, it does not suffice that the witnesses depose separately to divers acts from which the custom may be introduced, unless there are two at the least who have together seen each of the said acts <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>. The contrary opinion, then, is the sounder, and justly received by the sovereign courts, which will not judge rashly, but compass and measure all things by a straight ell, and weigh them in a just balance: especially in crimes, which, the greater and more horrible they are, the more must they be treated and determined with the greater circumspection and prudence <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>. And therefore one must conclude that in any crime whatsoever, however enormous it be, singular witnesses prove nothing; but it is necessary, to have certain and conclusive proof, that two (at the least) depose particularly to one and the same act <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup>. Nay, by the law, several singular witnesses would not suffice to condemn a man of heresy, even though he were defamed of it <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>. And in truth, inasmuch as this crime is the most grievous, and above all execrable, directly regarding the divine majesty, so much the more must the Judges look to it the more closely, that it be not judged by opinion and lightly, but rightly and in truth <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>; in order also to obviate the strange and prodigious conspiracies, calumnies and vengeance that many wicked men daily practise against good people under the cloak and pretext of religion <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>, with which they mask themselves, to cover their dissolutions, lecheries, thefts, extortions, and a thousand other kinds of wickedness and wretched impieties. Returning, then, to the matter from which we have strayed, it would not be reasonable that the depositions of witnesses who could not have been together at the fact to which they depose should be received as [those] of several <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 1.3 (De legibus senatusque consultis et longa consuetudine), l. De quibus (D. 1.3.32, Julian)
notes.original: l. de quibus. D. de legibus.
notes.gloss: Where written law fails, what has been introduced by usage and custom is to be observed; custom is the tacit consent of the people — Coras's "universal act".

notes.citation: Pierre de Belleperche (Petrus de Bellapertica, d. 1308, Pierre de Bellaper.) and Cino da Pistoia (Cynus, 1270–1336, Cyne) on Code 8.52 (Quae sit longa consuetudo), l. 2 (C. 8.52.2, Constantine)
notes.original: Pierre de Bella per. & Cyne en la l. ij. C. quæ ſit long. conſue.
notes.gloss: The commentators' requirement that a custom be proved by two witnesses at least who together saw each of the acts from which it is inferred, not by singular witnesses to separate acts.

notes.citation: Digest 48.4 (Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis), l. Famosi (D. 48.4.7, Modestinus); Liber Sextus, VI 1.6 (De electione et electi potestate), c. Ubi periculum (VI 1.6.3, Gregory X, the constitution of the Second Council of Lyons on the conclave)
notes.original: l. fameſi. D. ad l. Iuli. maieſta. c. vbi periculum de elec. au vj.
notes.gloss: D. 48.4.7.3: the crime of treason is not to be entertained by judges as an occasion of flattering the prince's majesty, but in truth; the greater the matter, the greater the caution — Ubi periculum maius intenditur, ibi procul dubio est plenius consulendum, the opening words of Gregory X's constitution, which Coras's "the greater and more horrible … the greater circumspection" renders.

notes.gloss: Singular witnesses do not convict of heresy even a man defamed of it.

notes.citation: Digest 48.4.7 (Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. Famosi), cited above at {n}
notes.gloss: Non in occasione … sed in veritate: the crime is to be judged in truth, not upon opinion.

notes.original: Clem. j ſur le commencé ment de haré.
notes.gloss: Clement V's constitution restraining the abuses of inquisitors, who had turned the office against the innocent; the print's haré. is hære[ticis].

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 3 q. 9, c. Nihilominus, cited above at {k}
notes.gloss: Witnesses who were not together at the fact are not several witnesses to it.
